obtained.how: the publisher's typeset PDF as posted by the Harkness Laboratory of Fisheries Research (Ontario MNR / University of Toronto; its list of contributions), 8 pages; Table 1 read on the page image

bibliography.checked_against: Crossref and the title page (PDF p. 1)
bibliography.note: authors, title, Behavioral Ecology 16(2): 427–434, doi:10.1093/beheco/ari006 all match. Crossref dates it 2004 (Advance Access 3 November 2004); the issue is 2005, as cited

claims.claim: at Opeongo guarding males lost little (585 to 571 g in 19 days; average-length males 2.4 % lighter, different fish at the start and end, not significant)
claims.location: p. 429 (PDF p. 3), Table 1 (page image); p. 431 (PDF p. 5), Results
claims.conditions: 2001; wet weights of an average-length male predicted from population-specific WW–TL regressions at the observed mean TL, from 12 males killed early in care (guarding unhatched embryos, 11 June) and 13 late (guarding free-swimming juveniles, 30 June); residual WW did not fall during care (F1,59 = 1.12, p = .29); (585 − 571)/585 = 2.4 %

claims.location: p. 429 (PDF p. 3), Table 1 (page image); p. 431 (PDF p. 5)
claims.quote: Smallmouth bass starting WW (g) 852 ... ending WW (g) 754
claims.conditions: Bass Islands, western Lake Erie, 1999–2000; 17 days of care (13–30 June); regression-predicted weights of an average-length male (19 early, 20 late males); (852 − 754)/852 = 11.5 % of wet weight; whole-body energy content fell 11 % (p. 431)

claims.claim: hyperabundant invasive round gobies raised the males' chase rate ninefold
claims.quote: chased predators nine times more frequently than smallmouth bass in Lake Opeongo
claims.conditions: 15 min of video per nest between 09:00 and 16:00, nests holding unhatched or hatched embryos: Erie 40 males (284 chases), Opeongo 27 males (51 chases); > 99 % of predators confirmed on Erie videotapes were round gobies (Steinhart et al. 2004); the authors note different predator communities make the comparison imperfect

claims.claim: 64 % of guarding Opeongo males had prey in their stomachs
claims.location: p. 431 (PDF p. 5), Diet of guarding males
claims.quote: had prey in their stomach in Lake Opeongo (64%) than in Lake Erie (21%)
claims.conditions: males angled from their nests (Opeongo, 2001) or taken by divers (Erie); prey > 5 mm identified; 50 % of males guarding embryos and 77 % guarding juveniles had eaten (Erie 5 % and 30 %)

claims.claim: guarding males eat little but rarely nothing
claims.source_value: eating nothing was common: 36 % of guarding Opeongo males and 79 % of Lake Erie males had empty stomachs; early in care (guarding embryos) 50 % of Opeongo and 95 % of Erie males had eaten nothing
claims.location: p. 431 (PDF p. 5), Diet of guarding males
claims.quote: males guarding embryos (Lake Erie: 5%; Lake Opeongo: 50%)
claims.conditions: stomach contents at capture, a snapshot; daily ration (Eggers model) rose from early to late care in both lakes
claims.note: "eat little" is the authors' own reading ("consumed few prey", abstract); "rarely nothing" is not: say "about two-thirds of Opeongo guards held prey (half early in care, three-quarters late)"

claims.location: p. 432 (PDF p. 6), Bioenergetic simulations; abstract p. 427
claims.quote: in Lake Opeongo, males had an ACT of 1.2
claims.conditions: ACT is a multiplier on standard metabolism in Fish Bioenergetics 3.0 with the Whitledge et al. (2003) adult smallmouth parameters, fitted so the model reproduced the measured end-of-care weight over the whole care period (embryos to free-swimming juveniles, 17–19 d); Opeongo, without round gobies. The abstract gives the Opeongo rise as 28 % and the Erie rise (ACT 3.1) as 210 %
claims.note: the source's own 1.2 and "28 %" disagree slightly (hence the code's 1.2–1.28). It is a whole-guard average for a low-predator lake; the code's staging (×1.4 early, ×1.12 late) is not from this source

notes: Internal slip in the source: p. 432 says a 350-mm Erie male spends 381 kJ "over 19 days" and an Opeongo male 53 kJ "over 17 days", but Table 1 and the methods give Erie 17 days (13–30 June) and Opeongo 19 days (11–30 June); the day counts in that sentence are swapped. Other values: Erie males lost about 20 kJ per day of care and spent more than six times the energy per day of Opeongo males; with Erie's ACT, Opeongo's cost would be nearly the same as Erie's; nests at 2–4 m over cobble (Erie) and 1–2 m on cobble (Opeongo); care lasts up to 6 weeks (Coble 1975, cited); chases at Opeongo were mostly horizontal (68 %), at predators in the water column (smallmouth, yellow perch, pumpkinseed); in Erie, round gobies can eat 400–2,000 offspring within 5 min of a male's removal and a whole brood in ~15 min (Steinhart et al. 2004, cited).
